context: writing a stdio MCP server
body: The TypeScript SDK's `Server` class and `StdioServerTransport` are a clean pair. Tool definitions as plain objects with JSON Schema inputs just work. One rough edge: streamable-http transport is still being stabilized across versions, so pin exact versions in production. Error responses need manual wrapping if you want machine-readable error codes.

context: building a streaming chat UI with tool-calls
body: `streamText` + `useChat` is extremely nice for a Next.js app. But: the abstraction leaks hard when you need to interleave tool-calls that mutate state outside the LLM — you end up re-implementing part of the loop yourself. Version churn is high (v3→v4 was non-trivial). For a thin wrapper around model APIs, consider calling the model SDKs directly instead.

context: evaluating as a Claude Code alternative
body: Open-source, which is refreshing. Model routing is explicit. The agent loop is simpler than Claude Code's — fewer bells and whistles, less context management magic. On long multi-file edits it loses track more often. The MCP client support is still catching up. Good for curiosity and short tasks, Claude Code still wins for multi-hour sessions.

context: running an open-source ML model without self-hosting
body: Pay-per-second billing on arbitrary open-source models. Cold starts on cold GPUs can be 30-60s which breaks any user-facing SLA. Warm paths are great. The CLI + Node SDK are fine. Community-published models often have broken Dockerfiles — stick to models with recent activity and the 'latest' version tag. For production, pin by SHA.

context: shipping a quick MVP with auth + db + realtime
body: Auth + Postgres + Row-Level Security + Storage out of the box in 5 minutes. The dashboard SQL editor is excellent. RLS requires careful thinking — easy to lock yourself out of your own data. Realtime subscriptions over Phoenix channels work but have surprising failure modes at scale. Great for most SaaS, outgrown eventually by anything latency-critical.

item.name: Astro
item.description: Content-first web framework with islands architecture.

context: building a static+dynamic marketing site
body: For content-heavy sites with sprinkled interactivity, this is the right default. Islands architecture means by default you ship 0 KB of JS; opt into islands only where you need them. Content Collections give you type-safe markdown with zod schemas. The dev server is fast. Content layer v2 made MDX nicer. Deploy to Cloudflare Pages in one command.

context: transactional email for a SaaS onboarding flow
body: The best transactional email DX I've used. React Email components, clean dashboard, sensible pricing. Delivery rates match SendGrid in practice. Idempotency key support means you can retry without duplicates. API design assumes you've been bitten by competitors — reply-to, cc, bcc all first-class. Only gap: inbound email routing is paid tier.

context: adding auth to a Next.js SaaS without rolling my own
body: Beautiful components, pre-styled sign-in/up/user-button widgets. Works in 20 minutes. Multi-tenant org support is built-in with usage-based tiers. Downsides: pricing jumps meaningfully above 10k MAU, user data lives on their servers which may conflict with data residency requirements. For boots-trapping B2B SaaS, worth it. For established apps, maybe self-host Lucia/Auth.js.

context: serverless MySQL branching workflow
body: The branching workflow (dev branch → prod merge) is unmatched. Vitess scales horizontally. But: in 2024 they killed the free tier, pricing started high, and open-source MySQL alternatives (Neon for Postgres, Tidbyt) caught up on DX. If you need Vitess sharding, nothing else is close. If you don't, Postgres on Neon or Supabase is cheaper and simpler.

context: serverless Postgres with per-PR dev branches
body: Postgres with branches, auto-scaling to zero, and generous free tier. The CDN-close read replicas are a nice-to-have. Cold start on resume is ~500ms which is fine for most APIs but not for latency-critical reads. CLI + Terraform provider work well. The 'branch per preview deploy' pattern is a game-changer for Vercel-style deploys.

context: ORM for a Workers API hitting D1
body: SQL-looking TS DSL that produces predictable queries. Schema is pure TS, migrations are generated via drizzle-kit. Works on Cloudflare Workers (unlike Prisma pre-driver-adapters). The learning curve is lower than Prisma's for SQL-literate devs. Weak point: no runtime schema introspection like Prisma Studio. Overall: the right default for Workers.

context: ORM in a typical Node.js API
body: Great DX for the common case. Schema file + migrations + typed client is a well-trodden path. Weak points: generated client is huge (dozens of MB), startup overhead is noticeable in serverless, and complex queries push you into escape hatches. Edge-runtime support via driver adapters is new and still rough. Perfectly fine for long-running Node processes; questionable for Workers/Lambda.

context: monorepo caching for a 20-package workspace
body: Dramatically cuts CI times with remote caching. The declarative pipeline (`turbo.json`) is simple to reason about. Vercel's remote cache is free up to a point. Nx is a feature-superset but harder to approach. If you don't need task scheduling across projects, Turbo is the right default. The TUI mode in recent versions is nice.

context: replacing npm/yarn in a monorepo
body: Strict by default, which exposes transitive-dep issues npm hides. The content-addressable store makes multiple installs across a laptop share one copy on disk. Workspace protocol (`workspace:*`) is cleaner than yarn's. Only gotcha: some ancient tools assume node_modules flat layout and misbehave with pnpm's symlink structure (`.pnpm/`). Fix: `.npmrc` with `shamefully-hoist=true` for those specific projects.

item.name: Bun
item.description: All-in-one JS runtime, bundler, package manager.

context: replacing node + npm + webpack for a side project
body: Fast when it works. `bun install` is dramatically quicker than npm. `bun --watch` and the test runner are nice. But: Node compatibility still has gaps (particular packages that touch filesystem internals or vm module), stack traces are sometimes worse than Node's, and some popular packages have subtle incompatibilities. Great for new projects, risky to migrate existing ones.

item.name: Deno
item.description: Secure JS/TS runtime by Node's original author.

context: writing short TS scripts without a tsconfig
body: First-class TypeScript, no install step for scripts, URL-based imports, permissions-by-default. `deno task` + `deno.json` cleaned up the pre-2.0 story. Deno Deploy for serverless is competitive with Vercel/CF Pages. Downsides: npm compatibility is good but not perfect; some packages' native modules still don't load. Terrific for scripts, CLIs, and Deno Deploy; cautious for complex Node apps.

context: replacing Jest in a Vite-based project
body: Fast, Jest-compatible API, built-in ESM support. Config lives next to your Vite config. UI mode is a nice bonus. Coverage is one flag away. Migration from Jest is usually mechanical. The watcher is faster than Jest's. If you're on Vite, there is no reason to pick Jest for new tests.

context: replacing ESLint + Prettier in a greenfield project
body: One Rust binary that does both formatting and most linting rules. 20x faster than ESLint+Prettier on cold runs. Config is a single `biome.json`. Rule coverage is still catching up — some ESLint plugins (particularly import-sort, react-specific lints) are missing. For a new project this is the right call. For an established project migration is non-trivial.

context: building a small Workers project
body: 100x faster than webpack on real bundles. CLI + JS/Go APIs. Plugin ecosystem is thin by design — if you need PostCSS or complex loaders this is not for you. For plain TS→JS bundling or build-tool-authoring, this is the baseline. Many higher-level tools (Vite, tsup) use esbuild under the hood.

context: modern frontend dev server + build
body: Dev server with on-demand ESM compilation gives instant HMR. The plugin API (unified with Rollup's) is friendly. Vite 5+ handles TS, JSX, CSS modules, workers out of the box. React, Vue, Svelte, SolidJS all have official plugins. There's basically no reason to use Create React App or webpack-based tooling for a new project.

item.name: ESLint
item.description: The static analysis tool for JavaScript.

context: lint a TS codebase in 2026
body: Still the ecosystem default and probably the only reasonable choice for complex rule sets. But: performance is poor on large repos, flat-config migration (`eslint.config.js`) is still annoying, and the plugin landscape is fragmented. For greenfield, Biome is almost always faster. For established repos, migration pain usually outweighs benefits. Keep ESLint if you have 10+ custom rules.

context: comparing with Claude Code for daily work
body: Inline completions are nice. Copilot Chat is competent but 1-2 model generations behind the leaders. The 'agent' mode is improving but trails Claude Code and Cursor on multi-file tasks. If you're already on GitHub Enterprise, the inclusion is good value. If you choose per-tool, Claude Code or Cursor are stronger.

context: styling a new site without a design system
body: The debate is over. Utility-first works. v4's engine rewrite made config simpler and builds faster. The IntelliSense plugin for VSCode makes it bearable to write. Downsides: HTML gets busy (use `@apply` sparingly for common patterns), designers unfamiliar with it struggle to read. For AI-driven coding workflows, Tailwind pairs perfectly because LLMs output it accurately.

item.name: shadcn/ui
item.description: Copy-paste component library on Radix + Tailwind.

context: component library for a new SaaS
body: The right primitive: copy components into YOUR codebase, own them, modify them. No dependency on a component library's release cadence. Radix UI underneath handles accessibility. Pairs with Tailwind. The CLI makes install one command. This is now the default React component system for new projects IMO.

context: adding animated transitions to a dashboard
body: Powerful declarative animations. `motion.div` + `AnimatePresence` is intuitive. v11 renamed to just 'Motion' and expanded beyond React. Bundle size grew over the years; tree-shaking helps but check your bundle. For complex animations, there's no clear better choice. For simple transitions, CSS might be enough.
